claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed primarily by selective oxidation at grain boundaries.
Selective grain-boundary oxidation produces brittle intergranular oxide networks.
In oxidizing environments, a relatively continuous oxide scale forms on the surface and along grain boundaries.
The oxide scale formed under oxidizing conditions consists primarily of products of Al and Cr oxidation.
Thermal-expansion and volume-change mismatch causes the continuous oxide layer to become strained and eventually spall.
Oxide-scale spallation exposes the underlying matrix to rapid attack and promotes intergranular crack propagation.
Under reducing conditions, the alloy lacks a robust, continuous protective oxide scale.
The absence of a protective scale under reducing conditions permits localized subsurface oxidation or dispersed oxide precipitation within the matrix.
Subsurface or dispersed oxides locally embrittle the microstructure and nucleate microcracks.
Catastrophic failure can occur once a critical network of microcracks forms.
The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an fcc matrix.
The additive-manufacturing process may produce microsegregation and grain-boundary heterogeneity in the alloy.
Relative to the unexposed baseline, oxidizing exposure will produce a thicker, more continuous oxide scale, spallation, and widespread intergranular cracking.
Relative to the unexposed baseline, reducing exposure will produce less continuous surface oxide coverage but more localized subsurface oxidation, embrittlement, and microcracking.
Both oxidizing and reducing exposures will degrade mechanical properties, including fracture toughness or stress-rupture life, relative to the as-built baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies at 900–1100 °C for exposures longer than 100 hours under oxygen contents above 21% or below 1%.
Changing the gas atmosphere between the specified oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions is the controlled intervention proposed to reveal the governing degradation behavior.
A lack of significant atmosphere-dependent differences in oxide formation or grain-boundary damage would falsify the selective intergranular oxidation hypothesis.
Failure of mechanical-property degradation to correspond with the observed oxidation and microstructural damage would falsify the proposed causal mechanism.
